The Districts of the Common Republic

The districts inherited through the peace are to be represented within the republic rather than governed as outlying colonies. Commissioners are reconciling the Cape and Natal registers with the institutions of the raad. The eastern coastal possessions likewise enter the republic's territorial records, confirming the claims won through the earlier negotiations and campaigns. District government must now provide dependable accounts and offices for residents whose public obligations pass to the republic. The settlement is to bind these territories to the common state, with their communities represented through its ordinary administration.
Enter the districts into the republican registers.
Debate Dutch and Afrikaans Public Life

Fund a conference on schools, public language and the position of English-speaking residents within the republic. The raad will choose an educational programme, language requirements for public service, or municipal accommodation.
Language and Belonging in the Republic

The new government has adopted Dutch and Afrikaans as the foundation of its public institutions. English-speaking residents remain numerous in the ports and towns, where their schools, churches and commercial connections form an established public life. The raad has withheld recognition of English as a national community within the founding settlement. Ministers must now determine how those residents will participate in the republic and learn its public language. A funded language conference will put the competing proposals before the delegates.
Bring the language question before the raad.

English-speaking households have remained in the republic after the departure of the imperial administration. Their merchants and skilled workers are important to the ports and workshops, but nationalist delegates insist that a common government needs a common public language. Teachers propose Dutch and Afrikaans instruction, libraries and scholarships that would draw residents into republican life through education. Officials favour language requirements for public appointments, expecting compliance while risking resentment among those excluded from office. Municipal delegates instead ask for room to preserve local schools and congregations while conducting national business in the republic's language. The funded programme must establish how integration is to proceed. Neither nationality nor belonging can be settled by changing a heading on a register: households will judge the policy through their schools, livelihoods and dealings with the state.
Endow Dutch and Afrikaans schools and scholarships.

Preserve local institutions within the common public language.

Negotiate the Purchase of Portuguese Mozambique

Place a funded offer before Lisbon for its remaining Mozambique districts, from Terra de Boa Gente and the southern coast to the Zambezi and the northern ports. The Portuguese cabinet can reject the proposal. The deposited purchase price returns to the treasury if no agreement is reached.
A South African Offer for Mozambique

South African envoys propose the purchase of our remaining Mozambique possessions. They offer a substantial payment and a settlement of the administrative handover, presenting their ports and inland commerce as the foundation of a new regional system. Yet the Zambezi routes and northern harbours carry interests that cannot be measured in one treasury payment. Officers, merchants and ministers would see withdrawal as the surrender of an imperial position. The cabinet must weigh immediate revenue against the loss of sovereignty, prestige and future commerce. No treaty can be concluded without its consent. The envoys await an answer before instructing their commissioners to receive the districts.
Conclude the sale and settle the public obligations.
The ports and districts remain under Portuguese sovereignty.

Lisbon has agreed to the purchase. Commissioners will receive the districts still under Portuguese administration, reconcile public accounts and arrange the handover of offices and harbours. Republican officials now face a coast whose commercial routes stretch far beyond Pretoria. The Zambezi districts require inland communications, while the northern ports connect communities, merchants and shipping interests with established institutions of their own. The treaty establishes sovereignty, but government will depend on dependable roads, local records and arrangements with those communities. The purchase fund will pass to Portugal as the public offices are received. The raad must make this agreement work through ordinary administration, rather than treat the signature as the completion of its task.
Ratify the treaty and receive the districts.

The Portuguese cabinet has refused to sell its Mozambique possessions. Its reply regards the ports and river districts as an imperial obligation that cannot be exchanged for an immediate payment. Our delegation will return, and the purchase fund will be restored to the treasury. Commercial correspondence can continue, but a renewed territorial proposal must wait until relations and circumstances make further negotiations possible.
Recall the delegation and preserve the correspondence.
The ministries are rebuilding diplomatic correspondence after the rejected purchase.

The offer would preserve local government while binding it to republican diplomacy. Its rejection would leave the raad to decide whether commercial access justifies a campaign against the country controlling those routes.

Send the Republic's Delegation to Berlin

Fund representatives to present the republic's commercial and territorial interests at the continental conference. The mission will record its participation in the conference and maintain diplomatic correspondence with the European ministries.
The Republic at the Berlin Conference

Our delegates have entered a gathering at which European governments seek rules for commerce, navigation and territorial claims in Africa. The republic comes with ports, a victorious army and interests that the ministries can no longer dismiss as an inland dispute. Its representatives will defend access to markets and insist that claims require administration and agreement, rather than lines on an unexamined map. Participation gives Pretoria a place in the correspondence through which future disputes will be negotiated. It does not grant title to every neighbouring country. The ministers must return with arrangements that the raad can sustain through public offices, funded expeditions and treaties with the governments whose territories lie beyond our frontier.
Present our interests and establish the diplomatic mission.

The funded columns have entered the unclaimed districts adjoining our northwestern frontier. Surveyors will record routes and water supplies, while officials prepare the accounts and stations required to maintain the expedition. The arid country cannot be governed through a proclamation alone. Existing communities, herds and trading routes will shape where public offices and roads can be sustained. The government must provide dependable supplies and establish arrangements that allow households to remain through the difficult seasons. The raad now has to support what its expedition has begun, rather than leave the frontier to an unsupported line of posts.
Supply the stations and commission the district records.

The European ministries have opened their conference on African commerce, navigation and territorial claims. Our envoys report that the republic can present its interests through a funded mission. Ports and trading routes give Pretoria a practical stake in these negotiations, while the victory over Britain has made its government a power that the ministries must reckon with. Delegates will need travel funds, interpreters, legal advisers and the records of our treaties. The raad can commission them now or postpone the mission while retaining the opportunity to arrange representation through the ministry. Participation will strengthen the diplomatic foundation of later frontier conventions, whose terms must still be agreed with the governments concerned.
Fund the mission and dispatch our delegates.
Prepare further correspondence before committing the mission.
